text: What is the Septuagent? Hey everybody,
I'm Dan Mlelen. I'm a scholar of the
Bible and religion. And if you've heard
that word before and you haven't
understood precisely what it means, it's
a reference to ancient Greek
translations of the books of the Hebrew
Bible. Now, the word comes from a word
meaning 70, which has reference to a
tradition that comes from a text called
the letter of Aristas. And according to
this tradition, there was a solucid
ruler in Egypt in Alexandria named Tommy
II Philadelphia. And he wanted to
collect for the library in Alexandria
all the texts of all the different
societies of the world. And somebody
said, "Hey, we're going to need the
Jewish law as well, the first five books
of Moses, the Pentatuk." So they
requested somebody from Jerusalem come
and translate the text. And Jerusalem
sent six scholars from each of the 12
tribes of Israel, which means 72
scholars, down to Alexandria
to translate the first five books of
Moses, the Penetuk or the Torah into
ancient Greek. And it took them exactly
72 days. Each of them did it on their
own. And when they came together and
compared their translations, they
discovered they were word for word
identical, which was taken as a sign
that God had endorsed and approved this
Greek translation of the Jewish law.
Now, there are very few scholars these
days who think that this letter is at
all historical. It is widely understood
as a legendary account of the origins of
the Septuagent. And in addition to the
fact that the narrative talks about the
king and the librarian and the situation
in Jerusalem in ways that don't really
line up with what we understand the
circumstances to be in 3rd century BCE
Alexandria and Jerusalem.
We have done a lot of research into the
translation of the first five books of
Moses and they very clearly were not
executed under the curation of a single
source or authority. They very clearly
have very different translation
methodologies from one book to another
and seem to have been translated to
serve slightly different rhetorical
goals. So one of the things that a lot
of Septuagent scholars these days are
looking at is why precisely the
Septuagent was translated. For instance,
just last year this paper was published
in Currents in Biblical Research, which
is a wonderful journal that looks at the
state of the field related to a bunch of
different research questions, but it's
called Septuagent Origins, the state of
the question, and just surveys the
different theories that are out there
regarding why the Septuagent was
translated. And I think most scholars
these days would say while we probably
can't nail down the precise motivations
that contributed to the project of the
translation of the books of Moses and
the rest of the books of the Hebrew
Bible into Greek. Most likely it
originated internally in the needs of
Jewish communities living in Alexandria.
So they probably wanted access to the
Jewish law, the books of the Hebrew
Bible, but didn't understand Hebrew well
enough and so had things translated into
Greek. But there are other theories that
are out there as well. Now I mentioned
that Septuagent means 70 has reference
to this story, which means that
originally Septuagent only referred to
the ancient Greek translations of the
first five books of Moses. But between
the 3rd century B.CE and probably the
1st century B.C.E. if not a tiny bit
later. The rest of the books of the
Hebrew Bible were also translated into
Greek and those translations became
quite authoritative within Greco Roman
period Judaism. So the Greekeaking
Judaism of ancient Egypt and other parts
of a henistic Grecoman world and these
translations were also very important to
Christianity. In fact, the Septuagent
was the Jewish scriptures of the
earliest followers of Jesus, including
the authors of the New Testament. And
this would remain the situation all the
way down into the 4th century CE. It was
at the end of the 4th century CE that we
have a concerted effort to shift
priority to the ancient Hebrew versions
of the texts of the Hebrew Bible. And so
there were a lot of early Christians who
actually thought that the Jewish scribes
had corrupted the Hebrew texts and that
the ancient Greek translations were more
faithful to the original because they
were much more messianic and they could
find Jesus much more easily in the texts
of the Septuagent. Now this brings us to
the relationship of the Septuagent to
the Hebrew Bible. The authoritative
manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible for
scholars today are the Maseretic texts
and the representative one is the
Lenengrad CEX which dates to about 1,000
CE. This is the oldest complete copy of
the entire Hebrew Bible. The Septuagent
was translated over a thousand years
earlier than that. So it is based on
much earlier manuscripts but it is a
translation. So there are many ways that
the Septuagent diverges from the Hebrew
and we as scholars have to try to figure
out is this because they had a divergent
source text? Did their Hebrew
manuscripts read something differently
or is it because they interpreted a
manuscript that matches what we have
slightly differently. So there have been
a lot of debates regarding faithfulness
and translator exugesus and the theology
of the translators of the Septuagent
that have tried to account for what the
state of the Hebrew Bible manuscripts
was at the time of the translation of
the Septuagent. And the Dead Sea Scrolls
have provided an awful lot of help
because when we compare the manuscripts
of the Dead Sea Scrolls to the Maseretic
text and to the Septuagent, what we see
is that there are a number of
manuscripts that fit into a kind of
protomaseretic
tradition. There are other manuscripts
that fit into a Septuagent tradition.
And then there are others that don't
really fit into either of those
traditions. And so what this may
indicate is that these texts were
circulating in a variety of different
versions and some of them differed
significantly from others. So for
instance, the book of Jeremiah in the
Septuagent is 16th shorter than it is in
the Maseretic text. And we found some
fragments of manuscripts of Jeremiah
among the Dead Sea Scrolls written in
Hebrew that align with those passages as
they exist in the Septuagent where there
are passages that are omitted and the
passages that are there are in a
slightly different order. And so this is
taken by many scholars to be evidence
that the maseretic version of the book
of Jeremiah is a later secondary
expanded version of the book of Jeremiah
and the Septuagent preserves an earlier
shorter slightly different version of
the book of Jeremiah. And there are a
variety of different texts where this is
the case and then there are other texts
where the Septuagent very closely
matches what we have preserved in the
Maseretic text. So this is an ongoing
text critical research question and
project but it shows us that the
Septuagent is of significant textritical
value when it comes to trying to
understand the state of these texts and
manuscripts in different periods of
time. The Septuagent is phenomenally
valuable to us even if it is complicated
by the fact that we're dealing with a
translation and we don't necessarily
know precisely what the source text in
the Hebrew was. Now, if you would like
some publications to read on the
Septuagent to get to understand it
better, probably the most accessible
text is going to be Laneir and Ross' The
Septuagent, what it is and why it
matters. This is going to be the easiest
to read for the lay person. We also have
Job's and Silva's book, Invitation to
the Septuagent. The second edition was
published in 2015. This is also a very
good discussion. And then Jennifer Dyn's
the Septuagent. I believe this is from
almost 20 years ago if not a little
more. This is also a very good
discussion. And then on the more
technical side of things, Natalio
Fernandez Marcos's The Septuagent in
Context, introduction to the Greek
version of the Bible is going to be more
academic. And then there are a couple of
anthologies. The TNT Clark Companion to
the Septuagent, edited by James Akin, is
very good. The Oxford Handbook of the
Septuagent is going to be even better in
my opinion. It's edited by Allison
Salvon and Timothy Michael Law. Both of
whom, by the way, were supervisors of my
Oxford Masters thesis, which was on
textual criticism of the Septuagent. And
then a couple of additional books that I
think are very important. When God spoke
Greek, the Septuagent and the making of
the Christian Bible by Timothy Michael
Law is a wonderful discussion of how the
early Christians relied on the
Septuagent in understanding the Jewish
scriptures in articulating the text of
the New Testament. That's a wonderful
discussion. And then Tessa Rjack,
another phenomenal human being and
phenomenal scholar, wrote Translation
and Survival, the Greek Bible of the
ancient Jewish diaspora. if you want to
understand a really good theory of why
the Septuagent is the way it is and what
it was doing for Jews in the ancient
diaspora. So, there is an awful lot more
to say about the Septuagent, but that is
a quick and dirty introduction to what
the Septuagent is, where it seems to
have come from, and what scholarship you
can check out if you would like to learn
more. And the fit for this video is
